כִּֽי־יִקַּח אִישׁ אִשָּׁה חֲדָשָׁה (Devarim 24:5) means new to him, which leaves out a man who takes his divorcee back; a widow, or another man's divorcee, is included.

more.h: The month, and its first day
more.t: The חֹדֶשׁ is named from the renewal of the moon, and the whole thirty days are called חדש. The first day alone is also called חדש: מָחָר חֹדֶשׁ (Shmuel I 20:18), לֹֽא־ חֹדֶשׁ וְלֹא שַׁבָּת (Melachim II 4:23), וְהָיָה מִֽדֵּי־ חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 66:23), בַּשַּׁבָּתוֹת וּבֶֽחֳדָשִׁים (Yechezkel 46:3). But בְּיֽוֹם־ הַחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי (Shmuel I 20:34) is the month entire, and means the second day of the month; and חֹדֶשׁ יָמִֽים (Bamidbar 11:20) is a full month, thirty days. His father explains לֹֽא־חֹדֶשׁ וְלֹא שַׁבָּת of the whole thirty: neither a month has yet passed nor even a week since you saw him.

עַתָּה יֹֽאכְלֵם חֹדֶשׁ אֶת־חֶלְקֵיהֶֽם (Hoshea 5:7) is the month decreed upon them, the month of Av; and בְּחָדְשָׁהּ יִמְצָאֽוּנְהָ (Yirmiyahu 2:24) is the month decreed upon her, when she cannot be saved from the hand of those who seek her. His father reads בְּחָדְשָׁהּ as an infinitive: why do all who seek her not weary? because at every hour they find her in her renewing, as though she were only now beginning to run before them.

פרע.sense: Three senses: rebelling, holding off and setting aside; uncovering, of the head and its hair; and vengeance.

more.t: שִׁמְעוּ מוּסָר וַֽחֲכָמוּ וְאַל־ תִּפְרָֽעוּ (Mishlei 8:33); וַתִּפְרְעוּ כָל־עֲצָתִי (Mishlei 1:25), you set my counsel at nothing; פּוֹרֵעַ מוּסָר (Mishlei 15:32); פְּרָעֵהוּ אַל־תַּֽעֲבָר־בּוֹ (Mishlei 4:15). In the passive, בְּאֵין חָזוֹן יִפָּרַֽע עָם (Mishlei 29:18), and where it is done to others, תַּפְרִיעוּ אֶת־הָעָם מִֽמַּֽעֲשָׂיו (Shemos 5:4). The sense of all of them is המרי והריחוק והבטול, rebellion, holding off, and annulling.

Some take them from the usage of Chazal (Megillah 17a), one who reads the Megillah למפרע, out of its order, which is turning a thing backwards and reversed. So לֹֽא־ אֶפְרַע וְלֹֽא־אָחוּס (Yechezkel 24:14) is that He will not go back from what He has said.

כִּי פָרֻעַ הוּא כִּֽי־פְרָעֹה אַֽהֲרֹן (Shemos 32:25), uncovered in its evil deeds; וּפָרַע אֶת־רֹאשׁ הָֽאִשָּׁה (Bamidbar 5:18), he uncovers the hair of her head hidden under the veil; וְרֹאשׁוֹ יִהְיֶה פָרוּעַ (Vayikra 13:45), אֶת־רֹאשׁוֹ לֹא יִפְרָע (Vayikra 21:10), רָֽאשֵׁיכֶם אַל־ תִּפְרָעוּ (Vayikra 10:6), since a mourner uncovers his head and takes off his turban or his cap and his headdress. And גַּדֵּל פֶּרַע שְׂעַר רֹאשֽׁוֹ (Bamidbar 6:5), the pei with a segol: when the hair grows long it shows uncovered below the turban.
Some explain בִּפְרֹעַ פְּרָעוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 5:2) and כִּי הִפְרִיעַ בִּֽיהוּדָה (Divrei HaYamim II 28:19) from uncovering.

פַּרְעוֹת אויב is נקמות האויב, the vengeances taken of the enemy, and so he takes בפרוע פרעות בישראל and כִּי הִפְרִיעַ בִּֽיהוּדָה. The Targum of נְקֹם נִקְמַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Bamidbar 31:2) is אִתְפְּרַע פֻּרְעֲנוּת.

משׁל.sense: Two senses: to rule, with מֶמְשָׁלָה for dominion; and to speak a מָשָׁל, which is the likening of one thing to another and holds hidden matters in it.

more.t: וְיָשַׁב וּמָשַׁל עַל־כִּסְאוֹ (Zecharyah 6:13), he will sit and rule on his throne; וּמָֽשַׁלְתָּ בְּגוֹיִם רַבִּים (Devarim 15:6); מְשָׁל ־בָּנוּ גַּם־אַתָּה (Shoftim 8:22), rule over us; משֵׁל בִּגְבוּרָתוֹ (Tehillim 66:7). The noun is וּמָשַׁל מִמְשָׁל רַב (Daniel 11:3) with the mem in chirik, and with a heh or a tav added, הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הָרִאשֹׁנָה (Michah 4:8), לְמֶמְשֶׁלֶת הַיּוֹם (Bereishis 1:16), וּמֶֽמְשַׁלְתְּךָ בְּכָל־דּוֹר וָדֽוֹר (Tehillim 145:13).

הנה כָּל־ הַמֹּשֵׁל עָלַיִךְ יִמְשֹׁל (Yechezkel 16:44); עַל־כֵּן יֹֽאמְרוּ הַמּֽשְׁלִים (Bamidbar 21:27), therefore those who speak in proverbs say; מֹֽשְׁלֵי הָעָם הַזֶּה (Yeshayahu 28:14), which Yonasan took from the first sense and rendered שִׁלְטוֹנֵי עַמָא, the rulers of the people. The noun is לְהָבִין מָשָׁל (Mishlei 1:6), וַיִּשָּׂא מְשָׁלוֹ (Bamidbar 23:7), לְמָשָׁל וְלִשְׁנִינָה (Devarim 28:36), and where a man makes them, הֲלֹא מְמַשֵּׁל מְשָׁלִים הֽוּא (Yechezkel 21:5).

In מְשַׁל הַקַּדְמֹנִי (Shmuel I 24:13) the word is in the construct, and it means the proverb of the ancient proverb-maker; or else it is another pattern and not construct at all, and הקדמוני describes it.

נִמְשַׁל כַּבְּהֵמוֹת נִדְמֽוּ (Tehillim 49:13), likened to the beasts; וְנִמְשַׁלְתִּי עִם־יוֹרְדֵי בֽוֹר, and I am counted with those who go down to the pit; וָֽאֶתְמַשֵּׁל כֶּֽעָפָר וָאֵֽפֶר (Iyov 30:19), I have become like dust and ashes; and where one likens another, וְתַמְשִׁלוּנִי וְנִדְמֶֽה (Yeshayahu 46:5). So too זִכְרֹֽנֵיכֶם מִשְׁלֵי־אֵפֶר (Iyov 13:12).

הַמִּמְשָׁלִים לְבֵית אֲבִיהֶם (Divrei HaYamim I 26:6) means like their father's house in might, for they were mighty men of valour. The mem comes with a chirik, as in עֲתַלְיָהוּ הַמִּרְשַׁעַת (Divrei HaYamim II 24:7) and וְהֶֽעָרִים הַמִּבְדָּלוֹת (Yehoshua 16:9).

ארץ.sense: The earth, the whole world or a part of it; wider than תֵּבֵל, which is the settled lands, while ארץ takes in the wilderness with them.

more.t: אֶרֶץ וְשָׁמָֽיִם (Bereishis 2:4), with its six vowel points, is known: a name for the whole world or for some of it. It is more general than תֵּבֵל, since תבל holds all the settled lands and ארץ holds the wilderness and the settled together. Sometimes it is one particular land: אֶרֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם (Bereishis 41:41), הִנֵּה אַרְצִי לְפָנֶיךָ (Bereishis 20:15).
Some say the root of ארץ is רץ and the alef is added, and that it is called so because the sphere runs over it and goes about it continually.

It is used both ways, mostly feminine. Masculine in וְלֹֽא־נָשָׂא אֹתָם הָאָרֶץ (Bereishis 13:6), נֶעְתַּם אָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 9:18), אַךְ־בְּגוֹרָל יֵֽחָלֵק אֶת־ הָאָרֶץ (Bamidbar 26:55), שָׁרַץ אַרְצָם צְפַרְדְּעִים (Tehillim 105:30); and אָבַל אֻמְלְלָה אָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 33:9) has both in one. The plural is וּמֵֽאֲרָצוֹת קִבְּצָם (Tehillim 107:3), אַרְצוֹת גּוֹיִם (Tehillim 105:44).

Because the earth is low, a low place is called ארץ: רֻקַּמְתִּי בְּֽתַחְתִּיּוֹת אָֽרֶץ (Tehillim 139:15), which is the womb, and אוֹפַן אֶחָד בָּאָרֶץ (Yechezkel 1:15), meaning low against the ofanim above it.

זיז.sense: By its place the word is like זיו, radiance; others make זיז a beast of the field, or a name for every beast of the field.

more.t: וְהִתְעַנַּגְתֶּם מִזִּיז כְּבוֹדָֽהּ (Yeshayahu 66:11), where by its place the word is like זיו. Yonasan renders it מַחֲמַד יְקָרָהּ, the delight of her glory.

Some say it is the name of a beast of the field, as וְזִיז שָׂדַי עִמָּדִֽי (Tehillim 50:11) and וְזִיז שָׂדַי יִרְעֶֽנָּה (Tehillim 80:14); and some say זיז is a general name for every beast of the field.

On וְזִיז שָׂדַי עִמָּדִֽי, Rabbi Yehudah beRabbi Simon said the זיז is a great bird, and when it spreads its wings it darkens the disc of the sun, as it is written המבינתך יאבר נץ יפרוש כנפיו לתימן, is it by your understanding that the hawk soars and spreads his wings toward the south. And it is called זיז because it holds every kind of taste, מזה ומזה, from this one and from that.

סוף.sense: To come to an end and be finished off; from it סוֹף, the end of a thing, and the סוּפָה, the storm wind; and separately סוּף, the reed.

more.t: סָפוּ תַמּוּ (Tehillim 73:19), they are spent and finished; וְזִכְרָם לֹא־ יָסוּף (Esther 9:28), their memory will not come to an end; יַחְדָּו יָסֻפוּ (Yeshayahu 66:17); and where the verb takes an object, אָסֵף כֹּל (Tzefaniah 1:2). Their sense is ענין כליה, an end made of a thing. He notes that אָסֹף אֲסִיפֵם (Yirmiyahu 8:13) is not properly of this root but of אָסַף, as he wrote in the root beginning with alef, though its sense is theirs.

סוֹף דָּבָר הַכֹּל נִשְׁמָע (Koheles 12:13), the end of the matter; סוֹף כָּל־הָאָדָם (Koheles 7:2); וּמְצָאתֶם אֹתָם בְּסוֹף הַנַּחַל (Divrei HaYamim II 20:17). All of them are אחרית הדבר ותכליתו, the last of a thing and its finish.

The סוּפָה is not removed from this sense: וּכְגַלְגַּל לִפְנֵי סוּפָֽה (Yeshayahu 17:13), וּכְמֹץ גְּנָבַתּוּ סוּפָֽה (Iyov 21:18), וְגַלְגִּלָּיו כַּסּוּפָֽה (Yeshayahu 5:28), כְּסוּפוֹת בַּנֶּגֶב לַֽחֲלֹף (Yeshayahu 21:1). It too is an end made of things, being the winds and the quakings that move things swiftly and make an end of them.

וַתָּשֶׂם בַּסּוּף עַל־שְׂפַת הַיְאֹֽר (Shemos 2:3), she set it among the reeds by the bank of the river; קָנֶה וָסוּף קָמֵֽלוּ (Yeshayahu 19:6). It is the גמא. A larger kind grows on the sea bed at the roots of the mountains, and of it is said סוּף חָבוּשׁ לְרֹאשִֽׁי (Yonah 2:6). This too he will not remove from the first sense, since it may be named for withering quickly.

שׁאן.sense: To be at ease; the sense of all of them is השקט ושלוה, quiet and tranquillity.

more.t: The verb is found with its last letter doubled: שַׁאֲנַן מוֹאָב מִנְּעוּרָיו (Yirmiyahu 48:11), Moav has been at ease from his youth; וְשָׁקַט וְשַֽׁאֲנַן (Yirmiyahu 30:10); וְשַֽׁאֲנַן מִפַּחַד רָעָֽה (Mishlei 1:33), at ease from the dread of evil. All three are past, being with patach, the first root letter with a patach as well; and יַחַד אֲסִירִים שַֽׁאֲנָנוּ (Iyov 3:18) is said without a pause, with a kamatz under the nun because of the sheva of the alef.

לְעַשְׁתּוּת שַֽׁאֲנָן (Iyov 12:5) and נָוֶה שַֽׁאֲנָן (Yeshayahu 33:20), a quiet dwelling, have a kamatz under the nun; the plural takes a dagesh, הַשַּֽׁאֲנַנִּים בְּצִיּוֹן (Amos 6:1), וּבִמְנוּחֹת שַֽׁאֲנַנּֽוֹת (Yeshayahu 32:18), נָשִׁים שַֽׁאֲנַנּוֹת (Yeshayahu 32:9). וְשַֽׁאֲנַנְךָ עָלָה בְאָזְנָי (Yeshayahu 37:29) he wrote in the root שָׁאָה.
In כֻּלּוֹ שַׁלְֽאֲנַן וְשָׁלֵֽיו (Iyov 21:23) the lamed is added; or the word is compounded of שָׁלֵו and שַֽׁאֲנָן, and that, he says, is the right one.

זהר.sense: To warn and to take warning; and in another sense to shine, זֹהַר being brightness.

more.t: וְהִזְהִיר אֶת־הָעָֽם (Yechezkel 33:3), he warns the people; וְהִזְהַרְתָּה אֶתְהֶם (Shemos 18:20); וְלֹא הִזְהַרְתּוֹ (Yechezkel 3:18); and in וְהִזְהִירֹה (Melachim II 6:10) a heh stands in place of a vav. Of the one warned, חָיוֹ יִֽחְיֶה כִּי נִזְהָר (Yechezkel 3:21), אֶת־קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר וְלֹא נִזְהָר (Yechezkel 33:4), וְהָעָם לֹֽא־ נִזְהָר (Yechezkel 33:6), וְהוּא נִזְהָר נַפְשׁוֹ מִלֵּֽט (Yechezkel 33:5), all four with kamatz, past and passive, in the sense of one who did not know to take heed. Also וְיֹתֵר מֵהֵמָּה בְּנִי הִזָּהֵר (Koheles 12:12), be warned, my son. The sense of warning, he says, is known.

וְהַמַּשְׂכִּלִים יַזְהִרוּ כְּזֹהַר הָֽרָקִיעַ (Daniel 12:3), the wise shine like the brightness of the firmament, and כְּמַרְאֵה־ זֹהַר כְּעֵין הַחַשְׁמַֽלָה (Yechezkel 8:2). The sense is נגה, a shining.

שׁבת.sense: To cease and stop; and from it the שַׁבָּת, and שַׁבָּתוֹת for weeks, each week named from the Shabbos that falls in it.

more.t: אֵיךְ שָׁבַת נֹגֵשׂ (Yeshayahu 14:4), how the oppressor has ceased; שָׁבַת מְשׂוֹשׂ לִבֵּנוּ (Eichah 5:15); שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַֽשׁ (Shemos 31:17); וְיוֹם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִשְׁבֹּֽתוּ (Bereishis 8:22); וַיִּשְׁבְּתוּ שְׁלשֶׁת הָֽאֲנָשִׁים הָאֵלֶּה מֵֽעֲנוֹת אֶת־אִיּוֹב (Iyov 32:1). The sense of all of them is הבטלה והפסק הדבר, leaving off and the stopping of a thing. The nouns are כָּבוֹד לָאִישׁ שֶׁבֶת מֵרִיב (Mishlei 20:3), with six points, רַק שִׁבְתּוֹ יִתֵּן (Shemos 21:19), and on another pattern שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן (Vayikra 16:31).

וְֽהָֽיְתָה שַׁבַּת הָאָרֶץ לָכֶם לְאָכְלָה (Vayikra 25:6) is feminine and שֹׁמֵר שַׁבָּת מֵֽחַלְּלוֹ (Yeshayahu 56:2) is masculine. עֹלַת שַׁבַּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ (Bamidbar 28:10) goes as חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 66:23) and יוֹם בְּיוֹמוֹ (Vayikra 23:37).

more.h: A week, and the seven weeks
more.t: שֶׁבַע שַׁבָּתוֹת (Vayikra 23:15) is seven weeks of days, and עַד מִמָּֽחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת הַשְּׁבִיעִת (Vayikra 23:16) is the morrow of the seventh week. A week is called so because there is a Shabbos in every week; and because seven שבתות might fall without seven whole weeks of days in them, it says תְּמִימֹת תִּֽהְיֶֽינָה, they shall be complete, making forty-nine days. Chazal (Menachos 66a) expounded something else in why it says תמימות, and he holds his own is the plain sense of the pasuk. So too with the shemittah of years, each shemittah year being called שבת: since שֶׁבַע שַׁבְּתֹת שָׁנִים (Vayikra 25:8) might fall short of forty-nine years, it specifies שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים שֶׁבַע פְּעָמִים.

On רַהַב הֵם שָֽׁבֶת (Yeshayahu 30:7), with וּמִצְרַיִם הֶבֶל וָרִיק יַעְזֹרוּ before it, he reads the pasuk of Yerushalayim, who thinks to be helped by Egypt and that they will be strength to her; הם שבת means they will cease and stop from helping her. He says he gave a better explanation than this in the root יָשַׁב.

more.h: What Rabbi Yonah takes from it
more.t: Rabbi Yonah explained שָׂרוֹף יִשָּֽׂרְפוּ בַּשָּֽׁבֶת (Shmuel II 23:7) from this sense, בכליון חרוץ, with a destruction decreed, until no memory is left of them; and so they explained שֶׁבֶת חָמָֽס (Amos 6:3). He notes that he has explained both in the root יָשַׁב.

more.h: Putting a stop to a thing
more.t: Where the verb takes an object, אֲשֶׁר לֹא הִשְׁבִּית לָךְ גֹּאֵל הַיּוֹם (Rus 4:14), וְהִשְׁבִּית אֶת־הַכְּמָרִים (Melachim II 23:5), וְהִשְׁבַּתִּי חַיָּה רָעָה (Vayikra 26:6), אַשְׁבִּיתָה מֵּֽאֱנוֹשׁ זִכְרָֽם (Devarim 32:26), תַּשְׁבִּיתוּ שְּׂאֹר מִבָּֽתֵּיכֶם (Shemos 12:15). In the passive, וְנִשְׁבַּת גְּאוֹן עֻזָּהּ (Yechezkel 33:28), and the noun is שָֽׂחֲקוּ עַל מִשְׁבַּתֶּֽהָ (Eichah 1:6).

פרך.sense: Hardship and crushing; and separately the פָרֹכֶת, the curtain that screened the Aron from the Ohel Moed.

more.t: וַיַּֽעֲבִדוּ מִצְרַיִם אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּפָֽרֶךְ (Shemos 1:13) and לֹֽא־יִרְדֶּנּוּ בְּפֶרֶךְ לְעֵינֶֽיךָ (Vayikra 25:53), with six points, he glosses בקושי וברצוץ, with hardship and crushing. Chazal say (Chullin 46b) שתהא נפרכת בצפורן, that it should crumble under a fingernail.

וְעָשִׂיתָ פָרֹכֶת (Shemos 26:31) is a sheet that screened the Aron, to divide between it and the Ohel Moed. In the words of Chazal, ותלה בחופת בנו פרכיות שחורות, he hung black פרכיות in his son's chuppah, which are black sheets like the tents of Kedar.

שׁטר.sense: An officer set over others, שֹׁטֵר וּמֹשֵׁל (Mishlei 6:7), an officer and a ruler; of the sense itself he says only that it is known.

more.t: שֹׁפְטִים וְשֹׁטְרִים (Devarim 16:18), judges and officers, and וְשֹׁטְרִים לְשִׁבְטֵיכֶם (Devarim 1:15), officers for your tribes.

אִם־תָּשִׂים מִשְׁטָרוֹ בָאָֽרֶץ (Iyov 38:33) is from it, and he reads מִשְׁטָרוֹ as ממשלתו, his dominion. Others read it as כתבו, his writ, that is his decree and his statute, from the way Chazal speak of a שטר חוב, a bond of debt (Bava Metzia 1:6, 12b).

אחד.sense: One: אֶחָד הָיָה אַבְרָהָם (Yechezkel 33:24), Avraham was one. Because one is the least of number, a small quantity is called by it.

more.h: A few, and joined into one
more.t: כְּיָמִים אֲחָדִים (Bereishis 29:20), that is, they were in his eyes like a few days. וְהָיוּ לַֽאֲחָדִים בְּיָדֶֽךָ, and they shall be as one in your hand, he glosses מחוברים בדבר אחד, joined in one thing. Where the alef falls away, וְדִבֶּר־חַד אֶת־אַחַד (Yechezkel 33:30), one speaking with another.
הִתְאַֽחֲדִי הֵימִנִי (Yechezkel 21:21), which he glosses התבודדי באחד המקומות, take yourself off alone to one of the places.

אַל־תֵּחַד כְּבֹדִי (Bereishis 49:6), let my honour not be joined to them, has its root and its sense here, and he sets it on the pattern of אֵהָב (Mishlei 8:17), I will love. אַל־יִחַדְּ בִּימֵי שָׁנָה (Iyov 3:6) is better taken from חָדָה, of joy, its doubled dalet only setting the reading right, the word being stressed on the earlier syllable, as he wrote in the grammar.

אַחַת אֶל־אֶחָֽת (Shemos 36:12) would properly be אַחֶדֶת, the dalet dropping and the tav being the sign of the feminine. In his own view אחת is a word derived on its own and not from אחד at all, but from אח, as וְעָשָׂה אָח מֵאַחַד מֵאֵֽלֶּה (Yechezkel 18:10): אח said of the masculine and אחת of the feminine, since no feminine form from אחד is found anywhere. Yonasan translated that pasuk plainly, וְיַעְבֵּד לַאֲחוּהִי, and he shall do to his brother.

אנך.sense: Tin, and the plumb line made of it; at the end of the entry also אָנֹכִי הָאֵל (Bereishis 46:3), I am the Kel, where אנכי is simply אני, I.

more.t: עַל־חוֹמַת אֲנָךְ (Amos 7:7) he explains as בדיל, tin, the Arabic calling it by the same word: a wall built to a measuring line and to the plummet of judgment. וּבְיָדוֹ אֲנָֽךְ (Amos 7:7) is משקלת הבדיל, the tin plummet, for the builder's weight is made of lead or of tin, which he names in the vernacular פְּייומְבִּין, a plummet.

more.h: Rabbi Yonah on הִֽנְנִי שָׂם אֲנָךְ
more.t: He praises Rabbi Yonah's reading of הִֽנְנִי שָׂם אֲנָךְ (Amos 7:8), behold I am setting a plumb line, as being the same as וְשַׂמְתִּי מִשְׁפָּט לְקָו וּצְדָקָה לְמִשְׁקָלֶת (Yeshayahu 28:17), and I will make justice the line and righteousness the plummet.
לֹֽא־אוֹסִיף עוֹד עֲבוֹר לֽוֹ (Amos 7:8) means: I will no longer pass over his sins, but call him to account for them in judgment, judging them by the plumb line of judgment and the line of law.

נכה.sense: To strike, whether a man, a thing, or one hand against the other; and by extension to lay a place waste. Near it, נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם, lame in the feet.

more.t: וְהִכִּיתָ אֶת־כָּל־זְכוּרָהּ (Devarim 20:13), you shall strike every male of it; וְהִכִּיתָ בַצּוּר (Shemos 17:6), you shall strike the rock; וַיַּךְ הַבָּרָד (Shemos 9:25), the hail struck. Of hands, אַכֶּה כַפִּי אֶל־כַּפִּי (Yechezkel 21:22), I will strike My palm against My palm, and וַיַּכּוּ־כָף (Melachim II 11:12), they clapped hands. Of the tongue, לְכוּ וְנַכֵּהוּ בַלָּשׁוֹן (Yirmiyahu 18:18), let us strike him with the tongue.

וְיַךְ שָׁרָשָׁיו (Hoshea 14:6) is that it strikes its roots this way and that, meaning its roots go far off; the word is used as in וּמָחָה עַל־כֶּתֶף יָם־כִּנֶּרֶת (Bamidbar 34:11), and it shall reach to the shoulder of the sea of Kinneres.

more.h: Striking a city, not its people
more.t: וַיַּכּוּ אֶת־צִקְלַג (Shmuel I 30:1) is a borrowed use and means they tore it down, since the pasuk speaks of the city and not the people: it says in the same place מִקָּטֹן וְעַד־גָּדוֹל לֹא הֵמִיתוּ אִישׁ, from small to great they killed no man.

Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar wrote that מַכֶּה, with a segol under the kaf, is a masculine noun on the pattern of מַטֶּה, its plural in הַמַּכִּים אֲשֶׁר יַכֻּהוּ אֲרַמִּים (Melachim II 8:29), those who struck him; his father writes the same. Rabbi Yonah wrote that it is rather the plural of the feminine מכה, as חִטִּים from חִטָּה and שָׁנִים from שָׁנָה.

The feminine noun is מַכָּה, a blow: מַכַּת־חֶרֶב (Esther 9:5), a blow of the sword, and מָה הַמַּכּוֹת הָאֵלֶּה (Zecharyah 13:6), what are these blows. Close to the root's sense are נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם (Shmuel II 4:4), lame in the feet, and נֶאֶסְפוּ עָלַי נֵכִים (Tehillim 35:15), stricken men gathered against me.
פַרְעֹה נְכֹה (Melachim II 23:29) may be of this sense, called so because he was נכה רגלים, lame in the feet; Targum Yonasan renders it פַּרְעֹה חֲגִירָא, Pharaoh the lame.

מצח.sense: The forehead, עַל־מֵצַח אַֽהֲרֹן (Shemos 28:38), on Aharon's forehead; of the sense he says only that it is known.

more.t: וּמִצְחַת נְחשֶׁת עַל־רַגְלָיו (Shmuel I 17:6) is a plate of brass, called מצחת because it was shaped like the מצחה that girls wear on their forehead.

נזל.sense: To flow. From it the מַזָּלוֹת, the constellations, named so because they flow in their course.

more.t: Mostly the verb stands alone: הָרִים נָֽזְלוּ (Shoftim 5:5), the mountains flowed, and מַיִם זָרִים קָרִים נוֹזְלִֽים (Yirmiyahu 18:14), strange cold running waters. Where it takes an object, וְעַפְעַפֵּינוּ יִזְּלוּ־מָֽיִם (Yirmiyahu 9:17), our eyelids shall run with water, and וּשְׁחָקִים יִזְּלוּ־צֶדֶק (Yeshayahu 45:8), the skies shall pour down righteousness. All of them, he says, are ההגרה, a pouring out.

מִפָּנֶיךָ הָרִים נָזֹֽלּוּ (Yeshayahu 64:2), the mountains flowed down before You, stands as it does because of the pause, its dagesh only for the beauty of the word, like the dagesh of חָדֵלּוּ in פְרָזוֹן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל חָדֵלּוּ (Shoftim 5:7), the villagers ceased in Yisrael. Rabbi Yehudah filed the word under the root זָלַל instead; that is not right, he says, since nothing of this sense is found in that root.

לַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְלַיָּרֵחַ וְלַמַּזָּלוֹת (Melachim II 23:5), to the sun and to the moon and to the constellations: they are named from this root because they flow in their course. הֲתֹצִיא מַזָּרוֹת בְּעִתּוֹ (Iyov 38:32), can you bring out the Mazaros in their season, means the same as מזלות, or else it is the name of a star.

מין.sense: A kind: what resembles a thing and is of its own make, עֹשֶׂה פְּרִי לְמִינוֹ (Bereishis 1:11), making fruit after its kind.

more.t: Two pesukim and a line. עֹשֶׂה פְּרִי לְמִינוֹ (Bereishis 1:11) and אֶת־חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ לְמִינָהּ (Bereishis 1:25), the beast of the earth after its kind, of which he says מה שדומה לו והוא מתכונתו, what is like it and is of its own make.

חתן.sense: To join by marriage: the father of a man's wife is his חֹתֵן, her mother his חֹתֶנֶת, and he is חָתָן to them, as he is on his wedding day.

more.t: וְלֹא תִתְחַתֵּן בָּם (Devarim 7:3), you shall not make marriages with them; וַיִּתְחַתֵּן לְאַחְאָֽב (Divrei HaYamim II 18:1), he made a marriage bond with Achav; וְהִֽתְחַתְּנוּ אֹתָנוּ (Bereishis 34:9), make marriages with us. The father of a wife is חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה (Shemos 18:1), the חותן of Moshe, her mother חֹתֶנֶת, as in אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם־חֹֽתַנְתּוֹ (Devarim 27:23), cursed is he who lies with his wife's mother.

Rabbi Yonah held that a wife's brother is called חותן, father-in-law, to her husband, and so read מִבְּנֵי חֹבָב חֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה (Shoftim 4:11): Chovav is Yisro's son, since Reuel his father is called אֲבִיהֶן, their father (Shemos 2:18), which would make Reuel Yisro. He rejects it, because Moshe says to him וְהָיִיתָ לָּנוּ לְעֵינָֽיִם (Bamidbar 10:31), and you shall be eyes for us, and it was Yisro who was with them in the wilderness. The right view is that Chovav is Yisro and Reuel is Yisro's father, אֲבִיהֶן meaning their grandfather, the language calling a grandfather father and a grandson son.

בְּיוֹם חֲתֻנָּתוֹ (Shir HaShirim 3:11), on the day of his wedding, is the day a man becomes a חתן, and he is called so מפני הסמיכה אל חתנו, because of his being joined to his father-in-law. So קוֹל חָתָן וְקוֹל כַּלָּה (Yirmiyahu 7:34), the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, and וְהוּא כְּחָתָן יֹצֵא מֵחֻפָּתוֹ (Tehillim 19:6), like a bridegroom going out from his chupah.

He reasons that as a man was called חתן on his wedding day, so a baby was called חתן on the day of his milah, the root of the word being התחדשות השמחה, the renewing of joy, which the milah renews as the wedding does.

The angel sought to kill Moshe because he had not circumcised Eliezer his son. Moshe understood that it was for the milah and told Tzipporah to do it, being himself unable for the sickness already upon him. וַתַּגַּע לְרַגְלָיו (Shemos 4:25) is at Moshe's feet, as if to say: if it is this punishment that has made you ill, here is the blood of the milah. חֲתַן־דָּמִים אַתָּה לִֽי then means you have become to me today a bridegroom of blood, of my husband's killing; and when the blood reached his feet and the sickness left him she said חֲתַן דָּמִים לַמּוּלֹֽת, a bridegroom of blood for the circumcisions, and not for the blood of killing.

צין.sense: A marker, like a מצבה, a standing stone, set over a grave or for a sign on the roads.

more.t: מָה הַצִּיּוּן הַלָּז (Melachim II 23:17), what is that marker; וּבָנָה אֶצְלוֹ צִיּוּן (Yechezkel 39:15), he shall build a marker beside it; and הַצִּיבִי לָךְ צִיֻּנִים (Yirmiyahu 31:20), set up markers for yourself. The word is on the pattern of חִבֻּק יָדַיִם (Mishlei 6:10), a folding of the hands.

אדן.sense: A lord or master; and separately the אֲדָנִים, the sockets that the boards and the pillars were set into.

more.h: A plural that honours one man
more.t: לָכֵן יְשַׁלַּח הָאָדוֹן (Yeshayahu 10:16), therefore the Lord shall send; וַֽאדֹנִי זָקֵֽן (Bereishis 18:12), and my lord is old. The plural comes as a form of honour for one: אֲדֹנִים קָשֶׁה, a hard master, and אִם־אֲדֹנָיו יִתֶּן־לוֹ אִשָּׁה (Shemos 21:4), if his master gives him a wife. It comes without the yud too, יֹֽאמַר־נָא אֲדֹנֵנוּ (Shmuel I 16:16), let our lord say. The sense itself, he says, is known.

more.h: The yud of the honoured Name
more.t: The honoured Name is in the plural for honour, carrying one sign of plural only, as וְקָרַֽע לוֹ חַלּוֹנָי (Yirmiyahu 22:14), and he cut out windows for himself; or else the yud is the yud of relation, as the yud of מוֹכִיחַ אָדָם אַֽחֲרַי (Mishlei 28:23), one who reproves a man afterward.

Where the word is secular it takes a patach, הִנֶּה נָּֽא־אֲדֹנַי (Bereishis 19:2), behold now, my lords. But in וַיֹּאמַר אֲדֹנָי אִם־נָא מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ (Bereishis 18:3) it is kamatz, and Chazal are divided over it (Shevuos 35b): some say it is secular and was said to the greatest of them, and some say it is holy. So too in וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹט אֲלֵהֶם אַל־נָא אֲדֹנָֽי (Bereishis 19:18) they say it is holy.

בִּי אֲדֹנָי בַּמָּה אוֹשִׁיעַ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shoftim 6:15), please my lord, with what shall I save Yisrael, is kamatz and yet not in pause. He suggests the kamatz is because of the zakef, the word being secular, since Gideon did not yet know that he was an angel.

כִּכָּר לָאָֽדֶן (Shemos 38:27), a talent for the socket, and וּשְׁנֵי אֲדָנִים תַּחַת הַקֶּרֶשׁ הָֽאֶחָֽד (Shemos 26:25), two sockets under one board. The sockets were hollow and the tenons of the boards, and of the pillars, went into them and were held up by them. So על מה אֲדָנֶיהָ הָטְבָּעוּ (Iyov 38:6), on what were its sockets sunk, which he glosses יסודותיה, its foundations.

עדן.sense: Delight: וַיִּתְעַדְּנוּ בְּטֽוּבְךָ הַגָּדֽוֹל (Nechemiah 9:25), they took their delight in Your great goodness.

more.t: The noun הָֽיְתָה־לִּי עֶדְנָה, I have had delight, is תענוג, pleasure, and is the days of youth. Without the feminine heh, גַּן־בְּעֵדֶן (Bereishis 2:8), a garden in Eden, and כָּל־עֲצֵי־עֵדֶן (Yechezkel 31:16), all the trees of Eden. Four places where the word is pointed otherwise are the name of a city, which he treats in the grammar.

On הַמַּלְבִּשְׁכֶם שָׁנִי עִם־עֲדָֽנִים (Shmuel II 1:24) some say the pasuk is elliptical: who clothes you in scarlet and feeds you delicacies, and the Targum has וּמוֹבִיל לְכוֹן תַּפְנוּקִין, and brings you delicacies. Rabbi Yonah read it as clothing you in scarlet in the days of delights. He holds that one may not alter what is written: עדן is said of the clothing itself, for as good food is a delight to the body, so is fine clothing and whatever else gives the body pleasure.

With a mem added, וְיִתֵּן מַֽעֲדַנִּים לְנַפְשֶֽׁךָ (Mishlei 29:17), he will give delights to your soul, and וְהוּא יִתֵּן מַֽעֲדַנֵּי־מֶֽלֶךְ (Bereishis 49:20), he will yield the dainties of a king. The adjective is שִׁמְעִי־זֹאת עֲדִינָה (Yeshayahu 47:8), hear this, you who are given to pleasure.

וַיֵּלֶךְ אֵלָיו אֲגַג מַֽעֲדַנֹּת (Shmuel I 15:32) can be read as in joy and delight, since he chose his death over his life. Others read it as bound, and he holds that right: so הַתְקַשֵּׁר מַֽעֲדַנּוֹת כִּימָה (Iyov 38:31), of the bonds of Kimah, and so Chazal use the word of tying, ראשי מעדנים שלהן (Sukkah 13b), the ends of their bindings. Agag came in the bindings and chains he was held in. Rabbi Yonah read it of pleasantness, for his many delights and the greatness of his kingdom.

חבצל.sense: חֲבַצֶּ֣לֶת הַשָּׁר֔וֹן (Shir HaShirim 2:1), which he says is the flower Chazal call the ורד, the rose.

more.t: One line. The tav is the feminine tav, like the tav of שֽׁוֹשַׁנַּת הָֽעֲמָקִֽים in the same pasuk, the lily of the valleys; and the flower is the one called ורד, a rose, in the language of Chazal (Sheviis 7:7), רוז"א in the vernacular.

זיו.sense: בְּחֹדֶשׁ זִו (Melachim I 6:1) is the month of Iyar; זיו in the language of Chazal is brightness and shining.

more.h: Why the month is called so
more.t: Chazal say (Rosh Hashanah 11a) that it is called so משום דאית בה זיוא לאילני, because there is brightness in it for the trees, זיו in their language being הזהר והנגה, brightness and shining. So the Targum renders מִנֹּגַהּ נֶגְדּוֹ (Shmuel II 22:13) as מִזִיו יְקָרֵיהּ, from the brightness of His glory.

גמד.sense: A measure: גֹּמֶד אָרְכָּהּ (Shoftim 3:16), a gomed its length, which he explains as אמה הזרוע, the cubit of the forearm.

more.t: The adjective is וְגַמָּדִים בְּמִגְדְּלוֹתַיִךְ הָיוּ (Yechezkel 27:11), and gammadim were in your towers, which he explains as ננסים, dwarfs, men of short measure.

חרם.sense: To destroy utterly: killing, cutting off and ruin; and from it the חֵרֶם a man devotes. Separately a net for hunting, and חָרֻם, of a sunken nose.

more.t: וְאֵת כָּל־הַנְּשָׁמָה הֶֽחֱרִים (Yehoshua 10:40), he destroyed every soul; וְהַֽחֲרַמְתִּי אֶת־עָֽרֵיהֶֽם (Bamidbar 21:2), I will destroy their cities; and in the passive, זֹבֵחַ לָֽאֱלֹהִים יָֽחֳרָם (Shemos 22:19), one who sacrifices to gods is to be destroyed. The sense of them all, he says, is הריגה וכריתה והשחתה ואיבוד, killing, cutting off, destroying and loss.
אִֽישׁ־חֶרְמִי (Melachim I 20:42), the man of my ban, may be explained from this, and Targum Yonasan has גְבַר דְחַיָב קְטוֹל, a man liable to be put to death.

In וְהֶחֱרִים, said of אֵת לְשׁוֹן יָם־מִצְרַיִם (Yeshayahu 11:15), the tongue of the sea of Egypt, the sense is cutting and dividing, as in לְגֹזֵר יַם־סוּף לִגְזָרִים (Tehillim 136:13), who cut the Yam Suf into pieces.

more.h: A man already as good as dead
more.t: On כָּל־חֵרֶם אֲשֶׁר יָֽחֳרַם מִן־הָֽאָדָם לֹא יִפָּדֶה (Vayikra 27:29) Chazal say (Arachin 6b) that it speaks of a man going out to be killed: whoever pledges his valuation or his worth, or another's, owes nothing, since he is already as one dead, and a dead man has no valuation and no worth. So מוֹת יוּמָֽת, he shall surely die: once he is dead there is no redeeming him.

כָּל־חֵרֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל (Bamidbar 18:14), every devoted thing in Yisrael, and what a man devotes to Hashem of all that he has: though the thing itself is not destroyed, to the one who devotes it it is as though destroyed, since he will have no benefit from it.

Near to this are יָצוּדוּ חֵֽרֶם (Michah 7:2), they hunt with a net, יְגֹרֵהוּ בְחֶרְמוֹ (Chavakuk 1:15), he gathers him in his net, מִשְׁטַח חֲרָמִים (Yechezkel 26:5), a spreading place for nets, and מְצוֹדִים וַֽחֲרָמִים (Koheles 7:26): all of them nets and snares to hunt with. Separately אוֹ חָרֻם אוֹ שָׂרֽוּעַ (Vayikra 21:18), which Chazal explain (Bechoros 43b) of one whose nose is sunk between his two eyes, so that he paints both eyes at once.

זנה.sense: To play the harlot, and to stray after other gods: וְזָנָה אַֽחֲרֵי אֱלֹהֵי נֵֽכַר־הָאָרֶץ (Devarim 31:16), straying after the land's foreign gods.

more.t: כִּי זָֽנְתָה אִמָּם (Hoshea 2:7), their mother played the harlot; וְאַתְּ זָנִית רֵעִים רַבִּים (Yirmiyahu 3:1), you played the harlot with many companions; וַתִּזְנִים וְגַם לֹא שָׂבָֽעַתְּ (Yechezkel 16:28), which he glosses ותזני עמם, and you played the harlot with them. Of the heart and the eyes, אֶת־לִבָּם הַזּוֹנֶה and וְאֵת עֵֽינֵיהֶם הַזֹּנוֹת (Yechezkel 6:9), their straying heart and their straying eyes.

On וְזָֽנְתָה אֶת־כָּל־מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ (Yeshayahu 23:17) he says the pasuk had likened her, once her merchants had ceased from her, to a forgotten harlot, and now says she will be sought again for her hire: all the kingdoms will trade with her.

זְנוּת וְיַיִן וְתִירוֹשׁ (Hoshea 4:11), harlotry and wine and new wine, with a plural in וְנָֽשְׂאוּ אֶת־זְנֽוּתֵיכֶם (Bamidbar 14:33), you shall bear your harlotries. With a tav before it, וַיִּשְׁפְּכוּ תַזְנוּתָם עָלֶֽיהָ (Yechezkel 23:8), they poured out their harlotry upon her. With a nun in place of the tav, מֵרֹב זְנוּנֵי זוֹנָה (Nachum 3:4), the many harlotries of the harlot, which he also explains as זנונים, harlotries, with the middle letter of זנה doubled.

הִזְנוּ וְלֹא יִפְרֹצוּ (Hoshea 4:10), they strayed and shall not increase, stands without an object; but אַל־תְּחַלֵּל אֶֽת־בִּתְּךָ לְהַזְנוֹתָהּ (Vayikra 19:29), do not profane your daughter to make her a harlot, and וַיֶּזֶן אֶת־יֹֽשְׁבֵי יְרֽוּשָׁלַם (Divrei HaYamim II 21:11), he led the dwellers of Yerushalayim astray, take one.

שֹנא.sense: To hate; of the sense itself he says only that it is known. Some of the uses are not real hate at all, but being loved the less.

more.t: כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה (Bereishis 29:31), Leah was hated: he was not hating her, but because he loved Rachel more, Leah was called hated. So too הָאַחַת אֲהוּבָה וְהָאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה (Devarim 21:15), the one beloved and the one hated.

The one who hates, וְיָנֻסוּ מְשַׂנְאֶיךָ מִפָּנֶיךָ (Bamidbar 10:35), let those who hate You flee from before You; the one hated, גַּם־לְרֵעֵהוּ יִשָּׂנֵא רָשׁ (Mishlei 14:20), the poor man is hated even by his neighbour; and the adjective, הַבֵּן הַבְּכֹר לַשְּׂנִיאָה (Devarim 21:15), the firstborn son of the hated one, built like נְבִיאָה.

רכשׁ.sense: רֶכֶשׁ, swift beasts that are ridden; and רְכוּשׁ, everything a man owns, with the verb רָכָשׁ for acquiring it.

more.t: Rabbi Yonah wrote that they are the good horses over whom many years have not passed. He holds it may rather be some other beast we do not know, since one pasuk sets the couriers בְּיַד הָרָצִים בַּסּוּסִים רֹכְבֵי הָרֶכֶשׁ (Esther 8:10), by the hand of the runners on horses, riders of the רֶכֶשׁ, and another gives וְהַשְּׂעֹרִים וְהַתֶּבֶן לַסּוּסִים וְלָרָכֶשׁ (Melachim I 5:8), the barley and the straw for the horses and for the רֶכֶשׁ: it looks like a kind besides horses.

The noun covers all a man's money: the cattle he bought, silver and gold, and every movable thing. So וְאֶת־כָּל־רְכֻשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר רָכָשׁ (Bereishis 31:18), all his goods that he had gathered. And on תֶּן־לִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ וְהָרְכֻשׁ קַח־לָךְ (Bereishis 14:21), give me the souls and take the goods to yourself, he says נפש is the souls of the men, for he asked of him nothing but the people, and let him take the livestock and all the money.

רכס.sense: Height: the רְכָסִים are the high mountains, and the verb is raising a thing up to join it to what is above it.

more.t: וְהָרְכָסִים לְבִקְעָה (Yeshayahu 40:4), the רְכָסִים into a valley, which he takes as the high mountains; מֵרֻכְסֵי אִישׁ (Tehillim 31:21), from the pride of men and their haughtiness; and the verb from it, וְיִרְכְּסוּ אֶת־הַחֹשֶׁן (Shemos 28:28), that is, they raise the choshen to join it to the ephod, which is above it.

פצע.sense: To wound, which is a splitting: a blow that brings out blood. The noun is פֶּצַע, the wound itself.

more.t: הִכּוּנִי פְצָעוּנִי (Shir HaShirim 5:7), they struck me, they wounded me, and the noun פֶּצַע תַּחַת פָּצַע (Shemos 21:25), wound for wound. The sense is splitting, and he gives the word for it in the vernacular. The Targum Yerushalmi renders וַיְבַקַּע עֲצֵי עֹלָה (Bereishis 22:3), he split the wood for the offering, with ופצע קיסין לעלתא.
פְצוּעַ־דַּכָּה (Devarim 23:2) is one whose testicles have been split open, even one of the two.

פצה.sense: To open, and chiefly the mouth; and near to it, a second sense of redeeming, which is the opening of a man's prison.

more.t: וְאָנֹכִי פָּצִיתִי־פִי (Shoftim 11:35), and I have opened my mouth; פְּצֵה פִיךָ וֶאֱכֹל (Yechezkel 2:8), open your mouth and eat; and וּפֹצֶה פֶה וּמְצַפְצֵף (Yeshayahu 10:14), one that opens the mouth and chirps. All of them are a sense of opening.
פְּצֵנִי וְהַצִּילֵנִי (Tehillim 144:11), free me and deliver me, and הַפּוֹצֶה אֶת־דָּוִד עַבְדּוֹ (Tehillim 144:10), who frees David His servant: redemption, and the opening of the prison.

שׁלה.sense: To be at ease and untroubled, with שַׁלְוָה for that quiet; a second sense of error and misleading; and the שליא, the sac the child lies in.

more.t: שָׁלוּ כָּל־בֹּגְדֵי בָגֶד (Yirmiyahu 12:1), all who deal treacherously are at ease; the adjective שָׁלֵו הָיִיתִי (Iyov 16:12), I was at ease; and the noun וְשַׁלְוַת כְּסִילִים תְּאַבְּדֵם (Mishlei 1:32), the ease of fools destroys them.

His father takes לְדַבֵּר אִתּוֹ בַּשֶּׁלִי (Shmuel II 3:26) from the sense of ease, built like מְרִי: he was speaking with him in peace, and killed him; or else it means suddenly, and so Onkelos renders בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאֹם (Bamidbar 6:9) by בִּתְכֵף שָׁלוּ. He himself sets it in the second sense: in error and deceit they took him aside to speak with him, and struck him down.

לֹא תַשְׁלֶה אֹתִי (Melachim II 4:28), do not mislead me, and the Targum of שְׁגָגָה (Bamidbar 15:25) is שָׁלוּתָא. So וַיַּכֵּהוּ שָׁם הָאֱלֹהִים עַל־הַשַּׁל (Shmuel II 6:7), and he was struck there for the שַׁל, that is, for the error he made in laying hold of the Aron when the oxen shook it: even the Levi'im were given it to carry only on poles, and he was no Levi at all. Chazal darshened that the Aron carried its own bearers, so all the more itself.

בָּנַי עַתָּה אַל־תִּשָּׁלוּ (Divrei HaYamim II 29:11) he reads from the second sense: let there be no forgetting and no error among you in purifying the house of Hashem. Rabbi Yonah wrote it from the first: do not rest and do not be quiet until you have finished the purifying.

וּבְשִׁלְיָתָהּ הַיּוֹצֵת מִבֵּין רַגְלֶיהָ (Devarim 28:57). In the words of Chazal the שליא is the sac in which the child stands in its mother's womb, and it may be that the pasuk means by it the little children, as though they were in the שליא still, which is how the Targum has it, וּבִזְעֵר בְּנָהָא. Rabbi Yonah explained לֹא תַשְׁלֶה אֹתִי from this sense, and he holds that far from right.

שׁקט.sense: To be quiet and still; the sense of all of them is rest and repose, with שֶׁקֶט for that quiet.

more.t: אֶרֶץ יָרְאָה וְשָׁקָטָה (Tehillim 76:9) he glosses as fearing Hashem and growing quiet from making war on Israel, as the words just before it say that at His rebuke נִרְדָּם וְרֶכֶב וָסוּס, chariot and horse fell into a dead sleep.

Where the verb takes an object it gives rest: וְאֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם יַשְׁקִיט רִיב (Mishlei 15:18), one slow to anger quiets strife, and לְהַשְׁקִיט לוֹ מִימֵי רָע (Tehillim 94:13), to give him rest from the days of evil.

תער.sense: תַּעַר, a razor, of which he says only that it is known; and תַּעַר again for the scabbard, the sheath a sword sits in.

more.t: Of the first he says nothing but ידוע, it is known: וְהֶעֱבִירוּ תַעַר (Bamidbar 8:7), let them pass a razor over, תַּעַר הַגַּלָּבִים (Yechezkel 5:1), the barbers' razor, and יִקְרָעֶהָ בְּתַעַר הַסֹּפֵר (Yirmiyahu 36:23), he cut it with the scribe's blade. The other is the נדן, the sheath: וַיִּשְׁלְפָהּ מִתַּעְרָהּ (Shmuel I 17:51), he drew it from its sheath.

ערה.sense: Pouring out and emptying; uncovering, and the nakedness that may not be uncovered; joining one thing fast to another; and the moist green of grasses.

more.t: וַתְּעַר כַּדָּהּ (Bereishis 24:20), she emptied her pitcher, and וִיעָרוּ אֶת־הָאָרוֹן (Divrei HaYamim II 24:11), they emptied the chest: a sense of pouring and emptying. So תַּחַת אֲשֶׁר הֶעֱרָה לַמָּוֶת נַפְשׁוֹ (Yeshayahu 53:12), because he poured out his soul to death, and אַל־תְּעַר נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 141:8). He suggests תִּשְׁכְּרִי וְתִתְעָרִי (Eichah 4:21) may belong here, since a drunkard vomits when he has drunk much.

עָרוּ עָרוּ עַד הַיְסוֹד בָּהּ (Tehillim 137:7), lay it bare, lay it bare to the foundation in her, and עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ וְעֶרְוַת אִמְּךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה (Vayikra 18:7), you shall not uncover your father's nakedness or your mother's; כִּי־עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ בָּאתֶם לִרְאוֹת (Bereishis 42:12), you have come to see the nakedness of the land. He also sets את מקרה הֶעֱרָה (Vayikra 20:18) apart as a sense of its own and leaves it unglossed.

On וְאַתְּ עֵרֹם וְעֶרְיָה (Yechezkel 16:7), and you were naked and bare, he reads the pair as בערום ובעריה, in nakedness and in bareness; or else they are adjectives, and when the navi speaks of Knesses Yisrael he speaks now as of a male and now as of a female, as he set out in his grammar. That second reading, he says, is the right one.

Rabbi Yonah takes כְּמַעַר־אִישׁ וְלֹיוֹת סָבִיב (Melachim I 7:36) as from the side, the figures going round every side of each board, like מֵעֵבֶר אִישׁ לֹיוֹת in that same pasuk; and so he takes מִמַּעֲרֵה־גָבַע (Shoftim 20:33) as the side of the hill, where Targum Yonasan has מִמֵישָׁר גִבְעָתָא. It seems to him that Chazal read it from the sense of joining: Rabbah bar Shila said it is like a man joined to his לויה, a man cleaving to his wife face against face.

וְקִיר עֵרָה מָגֵן (Yeshayahu 22:6) he takes as a sense of joining: they fixed the shields against the wall to fight the city, and Targum Yonasan has וְעַל שׁוּר דְבַקוּ תְרֵיסִין. In the words of Chazal מעורה is attached. Rabbi Yehudah put both this and עַד־יֵעָרֶה עָלֵינוּ רוּחַ מִמָּרוֹם (Yeshayahu 32:15) into that sense; he himself reads the second as until a spirit is uncovered upon us, or from pouring, as אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת־רוּחִי (Yoel 3:1).

עָרוֹת עַל־יְאוֹר (Yeshayahu 19:7) is an adjective for the moist greens and grasses, built like בָּלוֹת וּמְטֻלָּאוֹת (Yehoshua 9:5). On this account מִמַּעֲרֵה־גָבַע is a place next to Geva where grass and herbs grew, named for their moistness, and וּמִתְעָרֶה כְּאֶזְרָח רַעֲנָן (Tehillim 37:35) is growing moist and green.

ישׁר.sense: Straight: of what pleases, it was straight in a man's eyes; the יָשָׁר is the upright man, מֵישָׁר is level ground, and the verb makes a way straight.

more.t: לַאֲשֶׁר יָשַׁר בְּעֵינָי (Yirmiyahu 27:5), to whom it was right in My eyes; כַּאֲשֶׁר יָשַׁר בְּעֵינֵי הַיּוֹצֵר (Yirmiyahu 18:4), as it was right in the potter's eyes; כִּי־הִיא יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי (Shoftim 14:3), for she is right in my eyes. And of going straight on, וַיִּשַּׁרְנָה הַפָּרוֹת (Shmuel I 6:12), the cows went straight.

more.h: The upright rule in the morning
more.t: On וַיִּרְדּוּ בָם יְשָׁרִים לַבֹּקֶר (Tehillim 49:15), the upright shall rule over them in the morning: the upright have rule and greatness over the foolish rich who love this world, of whom it says נִמְשַׁל כַּבְּהֵמוֹת נִדְמוּ (Tehillim 49:13), he is likened to the beasts that perish. In this world the fools rule the upright, as עָשִׁיר בְּרָשִׁים יִמְשׁוֹל (Mishlei 22:7), the rich rules over the poor; in the World to Come the upright are the rulers, and that is morning for them and evening for the rich. The rich wear away in Sheol when they die and leave the dwelling they had; the upright do not, for though the bodily form decays, the form of their soul stands forever.

וְהָיָה הֶעָקֹב לְמִישׁוֹר (Yeshayahu 40:4), the crooked shall become level ground. הוֹלֵךְ לְדוֹדִי לְמֵישָׁרִים (Shir HaShirim 7:10) he says of good wine, which goes down straight and is very pleasant to a man, and so יִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּמֵישָׁרִים (Mishlei 23:31).

Where the verb takes an object it straightens: יַשְּׁרוּ בָּעֲרָבָה מְסִלָּה (Yeshayahu 40:3), make a highway straight in the plain; הַמְיַשְּׁרִים אֹרְחוֹתָם (Mishlei 9:15), those who make their paths straight; and וְעַפְעַפֶּיךָ יַיְשִׁרוּ נֶגְדֶּךָ (Mishlei 4:25), let your eyelids look straight before you.

פדן.sense: אַפַּדְנוֹ is his palace; and פדן means a pair, so that פדן ארם is named for the two Arams, though some make פדן a field.

more.t: וְיִטַּע אָהֳלֵי אַפַּדְנוֹ (Daniel 11:45): the alef is an addition and the word means his palace, and in the words of Chazal a palace is called אפדנא. His father writes that the alef is a root letter and the nun the addition, from וְאָפַדְתָּ לוֹ (Shemos 29:5), and files the pasuk under the root אפד.

פדן is two in the language of Chazal, and the Targum of וַיִּקַּח צֶמֶד בָּקָר (Shmuel I 11:7) is פַּדַן תּוֹרַיָא, a yoke of oxen. So מִפַּדַּן אֲרָם (Bereishis 25:20) is named for the two places called Aram, Aram Naharayim and Aram Tzovah. There are also Aram Damesek and Aram Beis Rechov, but two of them lie near one another and it is those two that are paired; and the Aram across the river is Aram Naharayim.
Some explain פדן ארם as the field of Aram, for in the tongue of Yishmael a field is called פדן; his father writes so as well.

עבד.sense: To serve: service done for men, the service of Heaven, and the working of the land. עֶבֶד is the servant and עֲבֹדָה the work itself.

more.h: Who serves and who is served
more.t: The plain verb is used of the one who serves and of the one served alike, but the one served is joined to it by a beis, לֹא־תַעֲבֹד בּוֹ (Vayikra 25:39). So of the servant you say עובד אותו, he serves him, and of the master עובד בו, he works him. Onkelos takes וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם (Bereishis 15:13) as though it read ועבדו בם, and so rendered וְיִפְלְחוּן בְּהוֹן; it may also be read as it stands, the serving said of Israel and the affliction of Egypt.
עֲבֹדַת עֲבֹדָה (Bamidbar 4:47) he glosses as the song, which is the service of the korban.

וְעָבַדְתָּ לּוֹ אֶת־הָאֲדָמָה (Shmuel II 9:10), you shall till the land for him, and עֹבֵד אֲדָמָה (Bereishis 4:2), a tiller of the ground. Because a man's need of the land is so great, and he must be busy with it always, he stands to it as a servant before his master; and so וְנִהְיֶה אֲנַחְנוּ וְאַדְמָתֵנוּ עֲבָדִים לְפַרְעֹה (Bereishis 47:19), the land being as a servant to its owners. Its produce is named for the work done on it, וַעֲבֻדָּה רַבָּה מְאֹד (Iyov 1:3), a very great husbandry.

Two readings of מֶלֶךְ לְשָׂדֶה נֶעֱבָד (Koheles 5:8). Either the field, from the constancy of a man's work in it, is called worked though it is itself the one serving, as וְנֶעֱבַדְתֶּם וְנִזְרַעְתֶּם (Yechezkel 36:9), you shall be tilled and sown; or the lamed of לשדה means for the sake of, so that even the king is served only for the sake of the field, out of which comes what he gives and what feeds his armies. That second reading, he says, is the right one.

וַיַּעֲבִדוּ מִצְרַיִם אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (Shemos 1:13), the Egyptians made the Children of Israel serve, and וְהַעֲבַדְתִּיךָ אֶת־אֹיְבֶיךָ (Yirmiyahu 17:4), I will make you serve your enemies. לֹא הֶעֱבַדְתִּיךָ בְּמִנְחָה (Yeshayahu 43:23) he glosses as: I did not force you to come before Me with a meal offering.

לָכֵן יַכִּיר מַעְבָּדֵיהֶם (Iyov 34:25) is their deeds, as the Targum renders מעשה by עוּבְדָא; and without the added mem, וַעֲבָדֵיהֶם בְּיַד הָאֱלֹהִים (Koheles 9:1), their deeds are in Hashem's hand.

שׁרת.sense: To minister and attend upon another; of the sense itself he says nothing at all, the entry being the citations and their forms.

more.t: וְשֵׁרֵת אֶת־אֶחָיו (Bamidbar 8:26), he shall minister with his brothers; וַיְשָׁרֶת אֹתָם (Bereishis 40:4), and he attended them; מְשָׁרֵת מֹשֶׁה (Bamidbar 11:28), the attendant of Moshe, with וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ מְשָׁרְתוֹ (Shemos 24:13), and Yehoshua his attendant; and of a woman, מְשָׁרַת אֶת־הַמֶּלֶךְ (Melachim I 1:15), attending the king, where by rule the form should be משרתת. The noun is the vessels of the service, אֶת־כָּל־כְּלֵי הַשָּׁרֵת (Bamidbar 4:12).

שֹרת.sense: מַשְׂרֵת, a pan: the Targum renders מַחֲבַת, a griddle, by מַסְרִיתָא, and he gives the name in the vernacular.

more.t: One line, on וַתִּקַּח אֶת־הַמַּשְׂרֵת (Shmuel II 13:9), and she took the pan, identified by the Targum of מַחֲבַת (Vayikra 2:5).

גוח.sense: To bring forth and to go out; from it the river גִיחוֹן, and groaning, which is breath brought out.

more.t: כִּי־אַתָּה גֹחִי מִבָּטֶן (Tehillim 22:10), for You are my bringer-forth from the womb, built like גוֹזִי. Where the verb takes an object it brings out: כִּי־יָגִיחַ יַרְדֵּן אֶל־פִּיהוּ (Iyov 40:23), that he brings out, and מֵגִיחַ מִמְּקֹמוֹ (Shoftim 20:33), bringing out, though some say the word stands of itself and means going out from its place. Plainly going out: בְּגִיחוֹ מֵרֶחֶם יֵצֵא (Iyov 38:8), in its coming forth, and וַתָּגַח בְּנַהֲרוֹתֶיךָ (Yechezkel 32:2), you went out.

The river may be named from this, because it goes out and spreads far, being a great river, הַסּוֹבֵב אֵת כָּל־אֶרֶץ כּוּשׁ (Bereishis 2:13), that goes round the whole land of Kush. His father writes that it is the Nile of Egypt, called גִיחוֹן because it goes out and waters the land. The one by Jerusalem carries the name too, small though it is, and it is the one called שִׁלֹחַ, for Targum Yonasan renders אֶל־גִּחוֹן (Melachim I 1:33) by לְשִׁילוּחָא; or it is called so because it goes out to the gardens to water them.
חוּלִי וָגֹחִי בַּת־צִיּוֹן כַּיּוֹלֵדָה (Michah 4:10), where וגחי is והאנחי, and groan; this too belongs to the first sense, since a groan is the bringing out of breath.

נגח.sense: To gore: thrusting and striking with the horn, with נַגָּח for the ox that is given to it.

more.t: וְכִי־יִגַּח שׁוֹר אֶת־אִישׁ (Shemos 21:28), if an ox gores a man, and the adjective וְאִם שׁוֹר נַגָּח הוּא (Shemos 21:29), if it is a goring ox. Of men: בָּהֶם עַמִּים יְנַגַּח (Devarim 33:17), with them he shall gore the nations, and בְּךָ צָרֵינוּ נְנַגֵּחַ (Tehillim 44:6), through You we shall push down our foes; and of two who push at one another, וּבְעֵת קֵץ יִתְנַגַּח עִמּוֹ מֶלֶךְ הַנֶּגֶב (Daniel 11:40), at the time of the end the king of the south shall push at him.

חטם.sense: One word, אֶחֱטָם: to be long of nose toward someone, that is, to hold back anger, since the nose and wrath are both called חוטם.

more.t: One line, on וּתְהִלָּתִי אֶחֱטָם־לָךְ (Yeshayahu 48:9): for the sake of My praise I will lengthen My nose toward you, as the same pasuk says אַאֲרִיךְ אַפִּי, I will defer My anger.

שׁמד.sense: To be destroyed, and where the verb takes an object, to destroy; of the sense itself he says only that it is known.

more.t: A list of uses: וְנִשְׁמַד כָּל־הֲמוֹנָֽהּ (Yechezkel 32:12), all her multitude is destroyed, and וְלֹֽא־ יִשָּׁמֵד שְׁמוֹ מִלְּפָנָֽי (Yeshayahu 48:19), his name shall not be cut off from before Me; and where the verb takes an object, וְהִשְׁמַדְתִּי אֶת־בָּמֹֽתֵיכֶם (Vayikra 26:30), I will destroy your high places, and בְּמַטְֽאֲטֵא הַשְׁמֵד (Yeshayahu 14:23), with the besom of destruction. Of all of them he says only ידוע, it is known.

רגל.sense: The foot, and from it going on foot, רְגָלִים for times, and being habituated; and separately to slander, and to spy out a land.

more.t: לֹֽא־ רָגַל עַל־לְשֹׁנוֹ (Tehillim 15:3), he does not slander with his tongue, and וַיְרַגֵּל בְּעַבְדְּךָ (Shmuel II 19:28), he slandered your servant: the sense is informing and talebearing. It may be from רֶגֶל, the foot, since the talebearer is always going about and carrying words from this one to that one. Near to it is עֲלוּ וְרַגְּלוּ אֶת־הָאָרֶץ (Yehoshua 7:2), go up and spy out the land, which he likens to וַיָּתֻרוּ אֶת־הָאָרֶץ (Bamidbar 13:21), and they searched out the land.

שֵׁשׁ־מֵאוֹת אֶלֶף רַגְלִי (Bamidbar 11:21), six hundred thousand on foot, meaning that they went on their feet. בָּעֵמֶק שֻׁלַּח בְּרַגְלָיו (Shoftim 5:15) is that he did not ask for a beast to ride on, from the greatness of his running and his desire for the war; and וַיֵּצֵא הַמֶּלֶךְ וְכָל־הָעָם בְּרַגְלָיו (Shmuel II 15:17) is from the greatness of the fear and the worry. וְכָל־הָעָם אֲשֶׁר־ בְּרַגְלֶיךָ (Shemos 11:8) is those who go with you at your foot, and וּלְרֶגֶל הַיְלָדִים (Bereishis 33:14) is at their slow pace, their feet not being in a run.

וְלֹֽא־עָשָׂה רַגְלָיו (Shmuel II 19:25) he takes as a way of naming the hair of the nakedness, as וְשַׂעַר הָֽרַגְלָיִם (Yeshayahu 7:20); and לְהָסֵךְ אֶת־ רַגְלָיו (Shmuel I 24:3) is a way of naming the passing of water. Targum Yonasan takes וְלֹֽא־עָשָׂה רַגְלָיו as it sounds, rendering וְלָא שְׁטַף רַגְלוֹהִי, he did not wash his feet.

more.h: A good foot, and a count of times
more.t: On אֹֽתְךָ לְרַגְלִי (Bereishis 30:30), where Hashem blessed you at my foot, he explains it as with a poor man, of whom people say רגל טובה לפלוני, so-and-so has a lucky foot. שָׁלֹשׁ רְגָלִים תָּחֹג לִי בַּשָּׁנָֽה, three times you shall keep a feast to Me in the year, and כִּי הִכִּיתָנִי זֶה שָׁלשׁ רְגָלִֽים (Bamidbar 22:25), that you struck me these three times, are both of them times, and one and the same word.

וְאָֽנֹכִי תִרְגַּלְתִּי לְאֶפְרַיִם (Hoshea 11:3) has been read as הרגלתי, I taught to walk, with a tav in place of a heh; and the sense of being habituated is known from Chazal, where it is like custom. עֵין רֹגֵֽל (Melachim I 1:9) Targum Yonasan renders עֵין קַצְרָא, the launderer's spring, and רֹגֵֽל is from רֶגֶל, the foot, because those who wash clothes rub them with their feet.

עשׁת.sense: Bright and burnished, as of iron; and separately thought, from which eleven takes its name.

more.t: שָֽׁמְנוּ עָֽשְׁתוּ (Yirmiyahu 5:28), they are fat and sleek, which he glosses צחו וזכו, they are bright and clear. בַּרְזֶל עָשׁוֹת (Yechezkel 27:19) is iron that is clear and burnished, עָשׁוֹת being a description of the iron weighed like רָחוֹק, far, and קָרוֹב, near. It is the metal called in la'az אציי"ר, or the iron called in Arabic הינד"י. Yonasan renders בְּעַרְקִין דְבַרְזֶל, bands of iron, like וְגִיד בַּרְזֶל עָרְפֶּךָ (Yeshayahu 48:4), your neck a sinew of iron; and so the Chachamim speak of an עששית של ברזל, a lump of iron, heated before Yom Kippur.

עֶשֶׁת שֵׁן (Shir HaShirim 5:14), which he takes as like the clearness of ivory. On another pattern, לְעַשְׁתּוּת שַֽׁאֲנָן (Iyov 12:5), weighed like עַבְדּוּת, servitude: Iyov says of himself that he is לַפִּיד בּוּז, a torch of contempt, and that before this he was for the brightness and pleasantness of the quiet and untroubled, and now he is נָכוֹן לְמוֹעֲדֵי רָֽגֶל, ready for those whose foot slips.

אוּלַי יִתְעַשֵּׁת הָֽאֱלֹהִים לָנוּ (Yonah 1:6): He will be appeased and take thought for us, for the will lies in the thought. אָבְדוּ עֶשְׁתֹּנֹתָֽיו (Tehillim 146:4) is his thoughts; like it in Aramaic is וּמַלְכָּא עֲשִׁית לַֽהֲקָמוּתֵהּ (Daniel 6:4), the king thought and wished; and the Targum of כִּי־אַֽחֲרֵי מַחְשְׁבוֹתֵינוּ (Yirmiyahu 18:12), after our own thoughts, is בָתַר עַשְׁתּוֹנָתָא נְהַךְ.

more.h: Why eleven is named from thinking
more.t: לְעַשְׁתֵּֽי ־עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ (Zechariah 1:7), the eleventh month, and עַשְׁתֵּֽי ־עֶשְׂרֵה יְרִיעֹת (Shemos 26:7), eleven curtains: eleven is called so because it is the counter's thought, the first thing that rises in his heart to count after ten, ten being the end of the number. Rabbi Yonah explained the word from שתי, two, and he says he has broken his words in the grammar.

שֹום.sense: To put or set, and so to set the heart to a thing, to set ranks against a city, and to put paint on the eyes.

more.t: מִי שָׂם פֶּה לָֽאָדָם (Shemos 4:11), who set a mouth for man, and כִּֽי־ שָׂמוּ אֹתִי בַּבּֽוֹר (Bereishis 40:15), that they put me in the pit, the second accented on its last syllable against the rule. וְשָׂם דֶּרֶךְ (Tehillim 50:23) he takes as one who sets his way in the ways of Hashem, and אֲשֶׁר־ שָׂם לוֹ בַּדֶּרֶךְ (Shmuel I 15:2) as that he set his forces and his ranks in the way to fight with Yisrael.

אֽוֹ־ בִתְשׂוּמֶת יָד (Vayikra 5:21), a putting of the hand, he explains as a partnership, that each of them puts his money into the business; the mem is pointed with a segol against the rule, though the Hilali sefer in Toledo has a patach. And שִֽׂימָה ־נָּא עָרְבֵנִי עִמָּךְ (Iyov 17:3) is place now a pledge and be my surety, or place now a guarantor on your behalf, as the pasuk goes on מִי הוּא לְיָדִי יִתָּקֵֽעַ, who is he that will strike his hand with mine?

more.h: Setting the heart to a thing
more.t: אַל־ תָּשֶׂם אֶת־לִבְּךָ לָהֶם (Shmuel I 9:20), do not set your heart to them, and מִבְּלִי מֵשִׂים לָנֶצַח יֹאבֵֽדוּ (Iyov 4:20), which he reads as without setting it on the heart. So too וְיָשִׂימוּ וְיַשְׂכִּילוּ יַחְדָּו (Yeshayahu 41:20), they will set the heart, as the pasuk says הַגִּידוּ וְנָשִׂימָה לִבֵּנוּ (Yeshayahu 41:22), tell, and let us set our heart.

וְֽחַנְפֵי־לֵב יָשִׂימוּ אָף (Iyov 36:13) does not mean that they lengthen their anger, as Rabbi Yonah wrote, since one who is long in anger is appeased and leaves his anger, as is said of the measures of Hashem, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (Shemos 34:6), slow to anger. It means rather that they grow angry and enraged when Hakadosh Baruch Hu brings suffering upon them, and they do not cry out or turn from their evil way.

more.h: Ranks, and paint on the eyes
more.t: וַיָּשִׂימוּ עַל־הָעִֽיר (Melachim I 20:12) is that they set their ranks and their battles against the city, and so שִׂים ־לְךָ אֹרֵב (Yehoshua 8:2), set an ambush for yourself. וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ (Melachim II 9:30) is that she put paint on her eyes, the earlier word set later, as in וְאֶת־הָעִיר שִׁלְּחוּ בָאֵֽשׁ (Shoftim 1:8), they sent the city into fire; and some explain it as that she adorned them, and so שִׁית זוֹנָה (Mishlei 7:10), the adorning of a harlot.

more.h: Where the one who placed is not named
more.t: וַיִּישֶׂם בָּֽאָרוֹן (Bereishis 50:26), he was put in the coffin: by rule it should be וַיּוּשַֹם, with a small patach standing for a great one and the chirik in place of the shuruk. Some hold the word is sound and comes from another root, and means that the one who placed him placed him in the coffin, the placer being left unsaid, as in וַיֹּאמֶר לְיוֹסֵף (Bereishis 48:1), where the one who said is lacking.

יבם.sense: To take a brother's widow: the man is יָבָם to her, and she is יְבָמָה to him.

more.t: בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ (Bereishis 38:8), come to your brother's wife and take her in yibum: the one who takes his yevamah, who is his brother's wife, is called מיבם, one who does yibum, and he is called יָבָם to her, and she is יְבָמָה to him, as לֹא אָבָה יַבְּמִֽי (Devarim 25:7), he does not consent to take me in yibum. The wife of the yavam is likewise called yevamah to her, on account of her husband: הִנֵּה שָׁבָה יְבִמְתֵּךְ (Rus 1:15), your sister-in-law has returned.

more.h: The form the possessive is built on
more.t: יְבִמְתּוֹ and יְבִמְתֵּךְ, his and your sister-in-law, are not joined from יְבָמָה but from יְבֶמֶת, as he set out in the grammar.

צבא.sense: To make war against a place, and צָבָא for an army; also a fixed term of service and the end of it.

more.t: אֲשֶׁר צָבְאוּ עַל־יְרֽוּשָׁלָם (Zechariah 14:12), who made war against Yerushalayim, and וַֽיִּצְבְּאוּ עַל־מִדְיָן (Bamidbar 31:7), and they made war against Midyan. In לִצְבֹא צָבָא (Bamidbar 4:23) the noun is added for clearness only, since לִצְבֹא, to serve, would have been enough, as in וַתַּשְׁרֵשׁ שָׁרָשֶׁיהָ (Tehillim 80:10), it took root with its roots. Where the verb takes an object, הַמַּצְבִּא אֶת־עַם הָאָרֶץ (Yirmiyahu 52:25), and all of them are the gathering of a host.

more.h: The women who gathered at the Ohel Moed
more.t: בְּמַרְאֹת הַצֹּבְאֹת אֲשֶׁר צָֽבְאוּ פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵֽד (Shemos 38:8), with the mirrors of the women who gathered at the entrance of the Ohel Moed: the daughters of Yisrael would gather at the entrance of the Ohel Moed and bring in their hands even their own mirrors for the donation of the Mishkan.

אֱלֹהֵי הַצְּבָאוֹת (Hoshea 12:6), meaning the hosts above and the hosts below. Though strength and force lie with hosts when they agree in one heart and gather together, even so He is master and ruler over them all, and they succeed not by their own strength but by His strength and His will.

more.h: A set term and its end
more.t: הֲלֹֽא־ צָבָא לֶאֱנוֹשׁ (Iyov 7:1), has man not a set term upon the earth, and כָּל־יְמֵי צְבָאִי אֲיַחֵל (Iyov 14:14), all the days of my term I will wait, and כִּי מָֽלְאָה צְבָאָהּ (Yeshayahu 40:2), her term is filled: all of them are an end and a time. On וֶֽאֱמֶת הַדָּבָר וְצָבָא גָדוֹל (Daniel 10:1) some explain צָבָא as desire, from the Aramaic דִּֽי־הֲוָא צָבֵא הֲוָה קָטֵל (Daniel 5:19), whom he wished, he would kill; and the chacham Rabbi Avraham Ibn Ezra explains it from the first sense, that a great host appeared to Daniel in the visions of the night.

בצק.sense: Dough; and a foot that goes bare, since when the shoe wears through the foot cakes with mud like dough.

more.t: אֶת־ בְּצֵקוֹ טֶרֶם יֶחְמָץ (Shemos 12:34), his dough before it was leavened, and לָשׁוֹת בָּצֵק (Yirmiyahu 7:18), to knead dough, which he glosses עיסה, dough. וְרַגְלְךָ לֹא בָצֵקָה (Devarim 8:4) and וְרַגְלֵיהֶם לֹא בָצֵֽקוּ (Nechemiah 9:21) he takes as a foot bare without a shoe, and of the same sense as dough, because when the shoe is worn away the foot grows doughy with mud.

עסס.sense: To tread and pound; and from it עָסִיס, the juice that comes out by pressing.

more.t: וְעַסּוֹתֶם רְשָׁעִים (Malachi 3:21), and you shall tread down the wicked: the sense is treading and pounding. From it עָסִיס is named, as יִטְּפוּ הֶֽהָרִים עָסִיס (Yoel 4:18), the mountains shall drip juice, and מֵֽעֲסִיס רִמֹּנִֽי (Shir HaShirim 8:2), of the juice of my pomegranate; it is the liquid that comes out by squeezing and pounding.

פגר.sense: A corpse, which he defines as the body without its spirit; and as a verb, to be too faint to go on.

more.t: רַב הַפֶּגֶר (Amos 8:3), many a corpse, and כְּפֶגֶר מוּבָֽס (Yeshayahu 14:19), like a trampled carcass, and עַל־ פִּגְרֵי גִּלּֽוּלֵיכֶם (Vayikra 26:30), upon the carcasses of your idols. Of the sense he says only that it is known, and then defines it: הפגר הוא הגוף בלא רוח, the corpse is the body without spirit.

more.h: Why the pasuk adds the word you
more.t: On וּפִגְרֵיכֶם אַתֶּם יִפְּלוּ (Bamidbar 14:32), your own carcasses shall fall, he says the word אַתֶּם, you, is there to make the thing clear: had it said your carcasses alone, one would have understood the carcasses of their children.

אֲשֶֽׁר־ פִּגְּרוּ מִלֶּכֶת אַֽחֲרֵי דָוִד (Shmuel I 30:21), who were faint from going after David: they were weakened and weary and could not walk. The form may be a passive one whose chirik stands for a shuruk, as in וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ (Yeshayahu 60:11), your gates shall be opened; or the verb may stand without an object; or it may take one, meaning that they made themselves faint, showing themselves weak although they were not, so as not to go, since they were afraid and chose to sit by the baggage rather than go.

more.h: The day the talmidim were spent
more.t: Like it in the words of Chazal is יומא דמפגרי רבנן, the day the rabbanan were faint: on the day the talmidim were weak and weary from their learning and could not come to the beis midrash, they would call it by way of a figure יומא דשפמי, a day of the moustache, that is a day of idleness, like one who shaves the moustache only and takes no wage for trimming the moustache alone but only for the head or the beard.

בלה.sense: To wear out and waste away; from it בְּלוֹיֵ, worn rags, and בַּלָּהוֹת, terrors, the letters of בהלה, panic, turned about.

more.t: לֹֽא־ בָלוּ שַׂלְמֹֽתֵיכֶם (Devarim 29:4), your garments did not wear out, and אַֽחֲרֵי בְלֹתִי (Bereishis 18:12), after I am worn with age. Where the verb takes an object, בִּלָּה בְשָׂרִי וְעוֹרִי (Eichah 3:4), He has worn away my flesh and my skin, and וְלֹֽא־יוֹסִיפוּ בְנֵֽי־עַוְלָה לְבַלֹּתוֹ (Divrei HaYamim I 17:9), the sons of wickedness shall wear him away no more. The description is בָּלֶה, worn, weighed like רָוֶה, sated, as שַׂקִּים בָּלִים (Yehoshua 9:4), worn sacks. Of this sense too he takes חָשַׁקְתָּ נַפְשִׁי מִשַּׁחַת בְּלִי (Yeshayahu 38:17), בְּלִי being a noun weighed like שְׁבִי, captivity.

בְּלוֹיֵ מְלָחִים, worn rags, is written with one yud only, the yud of the last root letter, the yud of the plural being wanting in the writing; and with an alef, בְּלוֹאֵי הַסְּחָבוֹת וְהַמְּלָחִים (Yirmiyahu 38:12). Of their sense he says only that it is known.

לְעֵת עֶרֶב וְהִנֵּה בַלָּהָה (Yeshayahu 17:14), at evening time, and behold, terror, and בַּלָּהוֹת אֶתְּנֵךְ וְאֵינֵךְ (Yechezkel 26:21), I will make you terrors and you shall be no more. The lamed is lightened, and the word is the reverse of בהלה and בהלות, panic and panics.

שׁחר.sense: Black, which he says is charcoal; and separately the dawn, from which youth is named, and seeking early, and brightness.

more.t: עוֹרִי שָׁחַר מֵֽעָלָי (Iyov 30:30), my skin has turned black upon me, with the description וְשֵׂעָר שָׁחֹר צָֽמַח־בּוֹ (Vayikra 13:37), black hair has grown in it, and שְׁחוֹרָה אֲנִי (Shir HaShirim 1:5), I am black, and doubled, שְׁחַרְחֹרֶת (Shir HaShirim 1:6), swarthy. חָשַׁךְ מִשְּׁחוֹר תָּֽאֳרָם (Eichah 4:8) is blacker than black, and he says השחור הוא הפחם, the black is charcoal. So the Chachamim say one may write with שחור and with שיחור, the first charcoal and the second the vitriol used for ink.

וּכְמוֹ הַשַּׁחַר עָלָה (Bereishis 19:15), and as the dawn rose, and כְּשַׁחַר פָּרֻשׂ עַל־הֶֽהָרִים (Yoel 2:2), like dawn spread over the mountains. From this youth is called שחרות, as כִּֽי־הַיַּלְדוּת וְהַֽשַּֽׁחֲרוּת הָֽבֶל (Koheles 11:10), for childhood and youth are vanity, since the days of youth are likened to the morning as the days of old age are likened to the evening.

וְשָׁבוּ וְשִֽׁחֲרוּ ־אֵֽל (Tehillim 78:34), they returned and sought God, and אֵלִי אַתָּה אֲֽשַֽׁחֲרֶךָּ (Tehillim 63:2), You are my God, I seek You, and מְשַֽׁחֲרֵי לַטָּרֶף (Iyov 24:5), those who seek after prey. Some explain all of them as seeking and searching out, and even so they belong to the sense of dawn, because at dawn a man seeks and searches and takes account, since one who is eager for a thing rises early at dawn. So too from the sense of morning, וּלְבַקֵּר בְּהֵיכָלֽוֹ (Tehillim 27:4), to visit in His chamber.

more.h: Brightness, and a trouble not foreseen
more.t: אֲשֶׁר אֵין־לוֹ שָֽׁחַר (Yeshayahu 8:20) he glosses as having no brightness and no clearness. לֹא תֵֽדְעִי שַׁחְרָהּ (Yeshayahu 47:11) is that you will not know the time of its coming, for it comes suddenly, like a thing that comes at dawn, which a man does not feel until he sees it; and so בַּשַּׁחַר נִדְמֹה נִדְמָה (Hoshea 10:15), at dawn the king of Yisrael is utterly cut off. Rabbi Yonah explains לֹא תֵֽדְעִי שַׁחְרָהּ as that the way of its healing and of escape from it will not be made clear to you. His father reads חָשַׁךְ מִשְּׁחוֹר תָּֽאֳרָם from this same sense, the brightness of their form.

קרץ.sense: To cut off; and from it the winking of an eye or a lip in mockery, as though one were cutting them.

more.t: קֶרֶץ מִצָּפֹון (Yirmiyahu 46:20), a cutting from the north: the sense is cutting off and decreeing. In the passive, מֵחֹמֶר קֹרַצְתִּי גַם־אָֽנִי (Iyov 33:6), which he glosses נגזרתי, I was cut. So too in the Mishnah, where הביאו לו את התמיד, they brought him the tamid, and קרצו means he slaughtered it.

The moving of the eyes and the lips in mockery and scorn is named from it, as though one were cutting and breaking them: יִקְרְצוּ ־עָֽיִן (Tehillim 35:19), they wink the eye, קֹרֵץ בְּעֵינָו (Mishlei 6:13), winking with his eye, and קֹרֵץ שְׂפָתָיו (Mishlei 16:30), pursing his lips.

חמד.sense: To desire, and to covet what belongs to another; and as a noun, what is precious: a pleasant land, choice vines, the delight of the eyes.

more.t: חָמַד רָשָׁע מְצוֹד (Mishlei 12:12), the wicked desires the net, and וְחָֽמְדוּ שָׂדוֹת וְגָזָלוּ (Michah 2:2), they covet fields and rob them, and לֹא תַחְמֹד בֵּית רֵעֶךָ (Shemos 20:14), do not covet your fellow's house. In the passive it is נֶחְמָד לְמַרְאֶה (Bereishis 2:9), desirable to the sight, and הַנֶּחֱמָדִים מִזָּהָב (Tehillim 19:11), more desirable than gold.

אֶת־בִּגְדֵי עֵשָׂו בְּנָהּ הַגָּדֹל הַֽחֲמֻדֹת (Bereishis 27:15) he takes as garments of worth and desirable ones, and כִּי חֲמוּדוֹת אָתָּה (Daniel 9:23) as a man of חמודות, that is, one who holds great excellences and good qualities. So too מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ (Yechezkel 24:16), the delight of your eyes, and אֶרֶץ חֶמְדָּה (Yirmiyahu 3:19), a land of desire, and כַּרְמֵי־ חֶמֶד נְטַעְתֶּם (Amos 5:11), you have planted vineyards of delight.

more.h: Bread of delights, or hot bread
more.t: לֶחֶם חֲמֻדוֹת (Daniel 10:3) he takes as bread of worth. Rabbeinu Hai explained it as להם חם, bread that is hot, and like it in the words of the Chachamim, נפלה לאור ונחמדו בני מעיה, it fell into the fire and its innards were heated. So they too explained lechem chamudos, Rabbi Yehudah the son of Rav Shmuel bar Sheilach saying in the name of Rav that even warm wheat bread with olives they did not eat.

נפשׁ.sense: The soul; and from it the body, a person counted, the will and the desire, the dead, and the breath of the mouth; and to be refreshed.

more.h: Where it means the body or the person
more.t: Sometimes it comes in the masculine, when he means the body by it: אֶחָד נֶפֶשׁ מֵֽחֲמֵשׁ הַמֵּאוֹת (Bamidbar 31:28), one soul out of five hundred, and כָּל־ נֶפֶשׁ אַרְבָּעָה עָשָֽׂר (Bereishis 46:22), all the souls, fourteen. בַּרְזֶל בָּאָה נַפְשֽׁוֹ (Tehillim 105:18), the iron entered his soul, is said so because the soul is afflicted by the affliction of the body; and בְּגֹעַל נַפְשֵׁךְ (Yechezkel 16:5) he glosses as your body.

He calls the dead by the name nefesh, because the cause of death is the parting of the soul from the body: וְעַל כָּל־ נַפְשֹׁת מֵת לֹא יָבֹא (Vayikra 21:11), he shall not come near any dead souls, and הַנֹּגֵעַ בְּמֵת לְכָל־ נֶפֶשׁ (Bamidbar 19:11), one who touches the dead of any soul. So too מֵֽאֲשֶׁר חָטָא עַל־ הַנָּפֶשׁ (Bamidbar 6:11); and some of the Chachamim explained that same phrase of one who pained himself from wine, that he sinned against the desiring soul, withholding its desire from wine altogether.

Because she is the mistress of the will and the desire, he hangs the sin and the trespass upon her: נֶפֶשׁ כִּֽי־תִמְעֹל (Vayikra 5:15), a soul that commits a trespass, and וְנֶפֶשׁ כִּי־תֶֽחֱטָא (Vayikra 5:1), a soul that sins; and the touching of the body likewise, since the body acts in partnership with her. So אַֽל־תִּתְּנֵנִי בְּנֶפֶשׁ צָרָי (Tehillim 27:12) is in the will and desire of my adversaries, and לֶאְסֹר שָׂרָיו בְּנַפְשׁוֹ (Tehillim 105:22) is by his own will, without leave of the king.

It is said of the breath and the vapour that goes out from the mouth, נַפְשׁוֹ גֶּחָלִים תְּלַהֵט (Iyov 41:13), his breath kindles coals; and Ibn Ezra explained so לָכֵן הִרְחִיבָה שְּׁאוֹל נַפְשָׁהּ (Yeshayahu 5:14), therefore the grave has widened her throat. In the passive, שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַֽשׁ (Shemos 31:17), He rested and was refreshed, and וְיִנָּפֵשׁ בֶּן־אֲמָֽתְךָ (Shemos 23:12), that the son of your handmaid may be refreshed, that is, that his soul may rest.

וְשִׁלַּחְתָּהּ לְנַפְשָׁהּ (Devarim 21:14), you shall send her away to herself, is that she is to belong to herself and not stand in another's authority. And by way of a figure Hashem is said to swear בְּנַפְשׁוֹ, by His soul, as also אֲשֶׁר לֹא־נָשָׂא לַשָּׁוְא נַפְשִׁי (Tehillim 24:4).

בוא.sense: To come, and where it takes an object, to bring; the sun's going in, that is its setting; a covered way of naming marriage; and produce.

more.t: בָּא אָחִיךָ בְּמִרְמָה (Bereishis 27:35), your brother came with guile. Where the verb takes an object it is bringing: וְהֵֽבֵאתִי עֲלֵיכֶם (Vayikra 26:25), I will bring upon you, and וְהֵבִיאוּ בָנַיִךְ בְּחֹצֶן (Yeshayahu 49:22), they shall bring your sons in the bosom; and in the passive, כִּי הֽוּבְאוּ בֵּית יוֹסֵף (Bereishis 43:18), that they were brought to Yosef's house. The word is also used as a way of honour for what passes between man and wife, as וַיָּבֹא אֶל־הָגָר (Bereishis 16:4), and he came to Hagar.

more.h: A hired beast comes for its wage
more.t: בָּא בִּשְׂכָרֽוֹ (Shemos 22:14), it came for its hire: it came to the work for its wage and not for nothing as with a borrower, and therefore the one who hired it does not pay if it was broken or died, as a borrower does.

more.h: The suffix that means to him
more.t: בָּהֶם תְּֽבוֹאָתְךָ טוֹבָֽה (Iyov 22:21) is that good will come to you, אַל־ תְּבוֹאֵנִי רֶגֶל גַּֽאֲוָה (Tehillim 36:12) is let it not come to me, and כָּל־יַד עָמֵל תְּבֹאֶֽנּוּ (Iyov 20:22) is it will come to him: so through the whole simple form of this root, the suffix is read with a lamed, to. And in בֹּֽאֲכָה אַשּׁוּרָה (Bereishis 25:18), as you come toward Ashur, the kaf is not an added letter, as many have thought, but is addressed to one who knows the place; were it added, the Mikra would not say so throughout.

וּבָא הַשָּׁמֶשׁ (Koheles 1:5), and the sun comes in, and לֹֽא־ יָבוֹא עוֹד שִׁמְשֵׁךְ (Yeshayahu 60:20), your sun shall go in no more: the sense is the sun's entering and its going in. So קוּמִי אוֹרִי כִּֽי־ בָא אוֹרֵךְ (Yeshayahu 60:1), arise, shine, for your light has come in, is that the light you were led by until now has set, and from here on the glory of Hashem shines upon you. And where the verb takes an object, וְהֵבֵאתִי הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בַּצָּהֳרָיִם (Amos 8:9), I will bring the sun in at noon.

His father explains כִּֽי־ יָבוֹא כַנָּהָר צָר (Yeshayahu 59:19) from this sense, like the river that goes into the sea and is seen no more. It may also be taken as it sounds: when the adversary comes to make war on Yisrael, like a river that comes in a rush, the spirit of Hashem drives against him and destroys him.

וַֽאֲכַלְתֶּם מִן־ הַתְּבוּאָה יָשָׁן (Vayikra 25:22), you shall eat of the old produce, and כִּתְבוּאַת גֹּרֶן וְכִתְבוּאַת יָֽקֶב (Bamidbar 18:30), like the produce of the threshing floor and of the winepress: it is a name that covers every fruit fit for food, and is called so because it belongs to the year that is coming, while that of the year gone by is called עָבוּר. Rabbi Yaakov ben Elazar brought here וְהֵבֵאתָ (Shmuel II 9:10), and you shall bring in, accented on the syllable before the last although the word is a future, and אִישׁ יָבִא בְּפִרְיוֹ (Shir HaShirim 8:11), in the sense of produce; and he says there is no need to take them out of their own sense.

אמר.sense: To say, with אֹמֶר and אִמְרָה for what is said; sometimes saying in the heart, that is thinking; and separately a treetop, and to exalt.

more.t: כֹּה אָמַר (Shemos 11:4), thus said Hashem, and אַתָּה אֹמֵר אֵלַי (Shemos 33:12), you say to me. The nouns are אֵין אֹמֶר וְאֵין דְּבָרִים (Tehillim 19:4), there is no speech and there are no words, and אֲמָרַי הַֽאֲזִינָה (Tehillim 5:2), give ear to my words, and with an added mem, וְאֶת־ מַֽאֲמַר מָרְדֳּכַי (Esther 2:20), the word of Mordechai; of their sense he says only that it is known.

In the words אֶל־מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹֽר (Shemos 6:10), to Moshe, saying, the saying means to say it to Yisrael. But אֶמֶשׁ אָמַר אֵלַי לֵאמֹר (Bereishis 31:29), last night he said to me, saying, is the infinitive doubled upon the verb to strengthen the matter, and the more so where it comes after; and so אֹֽמְרִים אָמוֹר לִמְנַֽאֲצַי (Yirmiyahu 23:17), they keep saying to those who despise Me.

הַֽלְהָרְגֵנִי אַתָּה אֹמֵר (Shemos 2:14) is that you are thinking, and וַיֹּאמֶר לְהַכּוֹת אֶת־דָּוִֽד (Shmuel II 21:16) is that he purposed to kill him; so too הָאֹֽמְרָה בִּלְבָבָהּ (Yeshayahu 47:8), she that says in her heart, and אָמַרְתִּי אֲנִי בְּלִבִּי (Koheles 2:1), I said in my heart.

בְּרֹאשׁ אָמִיר (Yeshayahu 17:6), on the top of the highest bough, אָמִיר being the uppermost branch. From this sense he takes הֶֽאֱמַרְתָּ (Devarim 26:17) and הֶֽאֱמִֽירְךָ (Devarim 26:18), that you have raised Him up and made Him great; and so יִֽתְאַמְּרוּ כָּל־פֹּֽעֲלֵי אָֽוֶן (Tehillim 94:4), all the workers of iniquity raise themselves up and grow haughty. It may be that וּבִכְבוֹדָם תִּתְיַמָּֽרוּ (Yeshayahu 61:6) belongs here too, with the alef changed for a yud.

more.h: Or those two are plain saying
more.t: Some explain אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי־טוֹב (Yeshayahu 3:10), say of the righteous that it is well, from the sense of exalting, and he says it is right that it be of the sense of saying. He holds it possible to read הֶֽאֱמַרְתָּ and הֶֽאֱמִֽירְךָ as saying too: you caused it to be said that He should be a God to you, and He caused you to say to Him to be a people to Him and to walk in His ways.

נחר.sense: The nostrils, the two openings of the nose; and the snorting of a horse is named from them.

more.t: מִנְּחִירָיו יֵצֵא עָשָׁן (Iyov 41:12), from his nostrils smoke goes out, which he glosses הם שני נקבי האף, they are the two openings of the nose. From the nostrils the snorting is named: נַחְרַת סוּסָיו (Yirmiyahu 8:16), the snorting of his horses, and הוֹד נַחְרוֹ אֵימָה (Iyov 39:20), the majesty of his snorting is terror.

ריק.sense: To empty out, said of the vessel and of what comes out of it alike; empty, and for nothing; and to draw a sword out for battle.

more.h: Emptying, and what it is not
more.t: הֵם מְרִיקִים שַׂקֵּיהֶם (Bereishis 42:35), they were emptying their sacks, and עַל־הָאָרֶץ יָרִיקוּ (Koheles 11:3), they empty themselves upon the earth. This word is used both of the vessel and of what comes out of it, and in that it differs from הצקה, pouring, which is said only of what comes out of the vessel.

וְלֹא־הוּרַק מִכְּלִי אֶל־כֶּלִי (Yirmiyahu 48:11), he was not emptied from vessel to vessel. Of שֶׁמֶן תּוּרַק שְׁמֶךָ (Shir HaShirim 1:3), your name is oil poured out, he says the word may be a descriptive form with an added tav, and though its vowel is a patach we find others like it: יִסַּד בְּצִיּוֹן (Yeshayahu 28:16), he founded in Tzion, and לֵב הוּתַל (Yeshayahu 44:20), a deceived heart.

כֵּלִים רֵקִים (Melachim II 4:3), empty vessels, and הַשִּׁבֳּלִים הָרֵקוֹת (Bereishis 41:27), the empty ears of grain. As a noun, וְתַם לָרִיק כֹּחֲכֶם (Vayikra 26:20), your strength spent for nothing, and וּלְאֻמִּים יֶהְגוּ־רִיק (Tehillim 2:1), peoples murmuring emptiness. With an added mem, רֵיקָם שִׁלַּחְתָּנִי (Bereishis 31:42), you would have sent me away empty handed, one form serving male and female alike.

וְחֶרֶב אָרִיק אַחֲרֵיהֶם (Yechezkel 5:2), I will draw a sword out after them, and וְהָרֵק חֲנִית (Tehillim 35:3), draw out the spear: he calls it arming for war. It may be near the first sense, since drawing a sword from its sheath is like emptying a vessel, and perhaps a spear too is given a sheath; and וַיָּרֶק אֶת־חֲנִיכָיו (Bereishis 14:14), he drew out his trained men, because they empty out the swords.

more.h: Like the mire of the streets
more.t: On כְּטִיט חוּצוֹת אֲרִיקֵם (Tehillim 18:43), like the mire of the streets I poured them out, he holds the quiescent letter stands in place of a dagesh, the word belonging to רקק in the words of Chazal, where a bird created מן הרקק, from the mire, is made fit by one sign; and the רקק is soft mud. Or the word may belong with וְרַקּוֹת בָּשָׂר (Bereishis 41:19), lean of flesh, and וּרְקִיקֵי מַצּוֹת (Shemos 29:2), thin matzah wafers, which is a sense of poorness.

בחר.sense: To choose, and what is chosen: choice silver, the choicest of a thing; and a young man, so called because he is chosen for work or war before the old.

more.t: כִּי־יַעֲקֹב בָּחַר לוֹ (Tehillim 135:4), for Yaakov He chose for Himself, and הַבֹּחֵר בִּירוּשָׁלָם (Zechariah 3:2), who chooses Yerushalayim; and where a man chooses, כִּי־בֹחֵר אַתָּה לְבֶן־יִשַׁי (Shmuel I 20:30), you are choosing the son of Yishai.

On בְּחַרְתִּיךָ בְּכוּר עֹנִי (Yeshayahu 48:10), I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction, Rabbi Yonah read the word as בחנתיך, I have tested you. There is no need for that, he says: a man chooses out the gold in the furnace from the dross.

more.h: The choice thing, and the young man
more.t: In the passive, וְנִבְחַר מָוֶת מֵחַיִּים (Yirmiyahu 8:3), death is chosen over life, and כֶּסֶף נִבְחָר (Mishlei 10:20), choice silver, a form Rabbi Yonah did not record. A youth is called בָּחוּר, a chosen one, because he is chosen for anything, for any work or for war, more than an old man: בָּחוּר וּבְתוּלָה (Yechezkel 9:6), young man and maiden; and the word serves a thing's best, בְּמִבְחַר קְבָרֵינוּ (Bereishis 23:6), in the choicest of our graves.
